docs.title: Verify Persistence
docs.text:
# List current models
docker exec $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") ollama list

# Restart container
docker restart $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest")

# Wait for restart
sleep 10

# Verify models still available
docker exec $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") ollama list

Expected Behavior: - Models remain available after restart - No re-download required - Same model list before and after

docs.title: Troubleshooting Persistence Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Models Lost After Restart

# Check mount configuration
docker inspect $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") | jq '.[0].Mounts'

# Verify host directory exists
ls -la /var/ollama/models/

# Check permissions
ls -ld /var/ollama
# Should show: drwxr-xr-x or similar

# Fix permissions if needed
sudo chmod 755 /var/ollama
sudo chown -R root:root /var/ollama

Problem: Models Corrupted After Restart

# Check for disk errors
dmesg | grep -i error

# Verify filesystem
sudo fsck /dev/sda1  # Adjust device as needed

# Restore from backup
sudo tar -xzf /backup/ollama/models-latest.tar.gz -C /var/ollama

docs.title: Check Storage Usage
docs.text:
# Overall disk usage
df -h /var/ollama

# Detailed breakdown
du -sh /var/ollama/*
du -sh /var/ollama/models/*

# Largest files
du -h /var/ollama/models/blobs/ | sort -h | tail -20

docs.title: Monitor Storage Growth
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# monitor-storage.sh

while true; do
  USAGE=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')
  USED=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $3}')
  AVAIL=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $4}')

  echo "$(date): Used: $USED | Available: $AVAIL | Usage: $USAGE%"

  if [ "$USAGE" -gt 80 ]; then
    echo "WARNING: Storage usage above 80%"
  fi

  sleep 3600  # Check every hour
done

docs.title: Storage Alerts
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# storage-alert.sh

THRESHOLD=85
USAGE=$(df -h /var/ollama | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | sed 's/%//')

if [ "$USAGE" -gt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
  echo "ALERT: Ollama storage usage at ${USAGE}%"
  echo "Consider removing unused models or expanding storage"

  # List models by size
  echo "Models by size:"
  docker exec $(docker ps -qf "ancestor=ollama/ollama:latest") ollama list

  # Send notification (example)
  # mail -s "Ollama Storage Alert" admin@example.com < /tmp/alert.txt
fi

docs.title: Deduplicate Blobs

Ollama automatically deduplicates model data using content-addressable storage. No manual deduplication needed.

Verify Deduplication:

# Count blob files
ls /var/ollama/models/blobs/ | wc -l

# Check for shared blobs between models
# (Blobs with same SHA256 are shared)

docs.text: TO: IBM Leadership & Product Teams FROM: Ikigai Team SUBJECT: Value Proposition of Model Context Protocol (MCP) Servers for IBM Products DATE: September 10, 2025

docs.title: Value Proposition: MCP Servers for IBM Products
Executive Summary
docs.text: The implementation of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for IBM products such as NS1, SevOne, Open Horizon, and others represents a strategic opportunity to enhance product capabilities, improve customer experience, and drive competitive advantage. This memo outlines the key benefits and value propositions for both IBM and its clients. By exposing each product as MCP tools, clients gain a flexible, extensible and AI-ready integration layer that transforms how they access, automate and extract value from IBM's portfolio.

  13. Cross-Selling Opportunities

  15. Creates natural integration points between previously siloed product lines

  16. Increases average product adoption per customer by 25-30%

  17. Reduced Support Costs

  18. AI assistants handle Tier 1 support inquiries, reducing support ticket volume by 40%
  19. Customers solve problems faster with contextual AI guidance
  20. Lower training costs for both IBM staff and customer teams

docs.title: Value Added for IBM Clients
docs.text:
1. Simplified Product Interaction
  2. Natural language interface eliminates need to learn complex command syntax
  3. Reduces time-to-value for new users by 50-60%

  4. Democratizes access to powerful features previously limited to specialists

  5. Knowledge Democratization

  7. Reduces dependency on key personnel and institutional knowledge

  8. Enables junior staff to perform complex operations with AI guidance

  9. Operational Efficiency

  10. Tasks that previously took hours can be completed in minutes through AI assistance
  11. Automation of routine workflows through conversational interfaces

  12. Estimated 30-40% productivity improvement for common tasks

  13. Reduced Training Requirements

  14. New team members become productive faster with AI guidance
  15. Training costs reduced by 50-60% through just-in-time learning

  16. Continuous learning as AI provides contextual help during actual work

  17. Better Decision Making

  18. AI assistants provide data-driven insights and recommendations
  19. Complex system relationships are explained in understandable terms
  20. Enables more informed decisions through contextual understanding of systems

docs.title: Product-Specific Value Propositions
docs.text:
• NS1 with MCP - Enhanced conversational network automation:
  • Integrating NS1 with MCP transforms complex network configurations into conversational AI workflows, allowing agents to configure DNS and network settings in natural language. An AI orchestration framework (like LangChain) leverages NS1’s capabilities via the MCP layer to validate the configuration, significantly reducing human-induced errors and expediting network changes.

  • How it's different from a chatbot: A traditional network chatbot or AI Assistant could only answer questions about DNS, like retrieving the status of a zone. An MCP-enabled agent, however, can proactively monitor the network, detect an anomaly, and use NS1's capabilities via MCP to autonomously resolve the issue and report its actions. It moves from passive answering to active execution.

  • SevOne with MCP - AI-powered network observability:

  • By exposing SevOne's telemetry data through an MCP server, the network monitoring data is transformed into actionable insights via an AI agent. For example, an agent could use an MCP tool to retrieve specific network performance metrics, and a retrieval framework (like LlamaIndex) could find related network documentation. An orchestration framework (like LangChain) could then interpret all this data, enabling even non-specialists to identify and resolve network issues more accurately and efficiently.

  • How it's different from a chatbot: A legacy monitoring chatbot might provide a text response with a link to an outage report. In contrast, an MCP-enabled agent can actively monitor SevOne data, ingest a live streaming context of the network's health, correlate real-time anomalies with documentation via a RAG system, and initiate a self-healing action in another MCP-enabled system. The AI goes beyond simply retrieving a report and instead participates in resolving the incident.

  • Open Horizon with MCP: Exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server enables AI agents to autonomously deploy, update, and manage containerized workloads across large numbers of distributed edge devices. Unlike traditional chatbots which rely on static knowledge and require explicit user requests, an MCP-enabled agent can manage and reason across thousands of edge devices simultaneously using real-time data to make dynamic decisions and trigger self-healing actions or re-task devices based on changing needs

docs.title: Comparison: Model Context Protocol (MCP) vs. LangChain / LlamaIndex
docs.text:
When comparing MCP to other popular AI integration tools, it's essential to understand their distinct functions. MCP is a universal communication protocol, while LangChain and LlamaIndex are powerful frameworks built for specific tasks.

Feature Model Context Protocol (MCP) LangChain / LlamaIndex Fundamental Nature An open protocol defining a standard for communication, much like a "USB-C port for AI". A framework or library providing components and structures to build complex AI applications. Purpose Standardize connectivity between AI models and external tools or data sources. Orchestrate complex workflows and manage the internal logic of the AI application. Key Function Provides a standardized interface for accessing tools and data, abstracting away integration details. Offers building blocks for prompt management, chaining, data retrieval (RAG), and agent creation. Stability Protocol-based stability that is less susceptible to breaking changes, ensuring more reliable enterprise deployments. Library-based, with faster-evolving APIs and components, which can be less stable in production environments. Flexibility Offers flexibility through model-agnostic tool access. Any MCP-compliant AI client can use any MCP-compliant server. Offers high flexibility for customizing application workflows and defining multi-step processes within the framework. Best Used For providing standardized, plug-and-play access to a wide range of external tools and data sources. For building complex, stateful applications that require detailed workflow management, advanced reasoning, and memory. Typical Integration Can be used by frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex to simplify tool integration. Uses tools (which may be MCP-compliant) as components within its orchestration logic.

docs.title: MCP for Agentic AI Implementation
docs.text:
MCP serves as a vital foundation for implementing agentic AI systems within enterprise environments, particularly when scaling these systems securely and reliably.

  1. Tool-First Architecture
  2. MCP's tool-oriented design natively aligns with agent-based systems that interact with enterprise capabilities.
  3. Provides clear boundaries and interfaces for agent actions, giving agents a common language for using external resources.

  4. Enables fine-grained control over agent capabilities and permissions by managing access at the server level.

  5. Context Management

  6. MCP is designed for dynamic context exchange. It allows agents to pull the latest information from a source on demand, significantly reducing hallucinations and grounding responses in current, factual data. For example, an agent could use MCP to query the latest sales data before generating a report.

  7. Composable Actions

  8. Allows agents to combine multiple tools into sophisticated workflows, with the orchestration handled by a framework.

  9. Supports dynamic tool selection based on context and requirements, enabling the agent to intelligently decide which MCP-enabled tools to call.

  10. Enterprise Guardrails

  11. MCP's standardized protocol allows organizations to implement built-in security mechanisms and safety constraints on agent actions.
  12. It enables comprehensive logging and auditing of all agent activities that interact with external tools.

  13. Supports approval workflows for sensitive operations, as user consent is a key principle of the protocol.

  14. Scalable Multi-Agent Systems

  15. With the rise of the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, multi-agent systems now have a richer framework for collaboration. MCP often works in tandem with A2A.
  16. In this symbiotic relationship, A2A handles high-level coordination and communication between agents, while MCP manages the low-level interactions with tools and data needed by individual agents.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Implementing MCP servers across IBM's product portfolio creates substantial value for both IBM and its clients by enabling seamless and standardized integration of AI agents. This approach solidifies IBM's commitment to delivering enterprise-ready AI solutions, aligning perfectly with its broader AI leadership and client success strategy.

For IBM, standardizing on MCP drives competitive differentiation, increases product stickiness, and opens new revenue opportunities by enabling a cohesive, interoperable AI ecosystem.

For clients, it dramatically improves productivity, reduces the complexity of AI integration, and democratizes access to powerful product capabilities in a secure, governed manner.

The key to unlocking this value lies not in replacing existing frameworks but in adopting a synergistic approach. Instead of viewing MCP as a replacement for frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, the strategic advantage lies in combining them:

  • MCP provides the foundational, standardized "plumbing" for connecting AI agents to enterprise tools and data sources.
  • Frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex provide the higher-level orchestration, logic, and data handling required to build complex agentic applications.

By leveraging MCP for standardized tool access and relying on orchestration frameworks for complex workflows, organizations can build robust, scalable, and production-ready AI systems that deliver real business value. This strategic initiative enhances IBM's role as a trusted partner for enterprise AI adoption.

docs.title: Supercharging Open Horizon Management with Claude and IBM CodeEngine MCP: A Practical Guide
Introduction
docs.text:
In the rapidly evolving landscape of edge computing, managing distributed devices efficiently has become a critical challenge. Open Horizon, an open-source edge computing platform, provides powerful tools for deploying and managing workloads across edge devices. However, interacting with these tools traditionally requires specialized knowledge and command-line expertise.

Enter the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and large language models like Claude. Together, they transform how we interact with complex systems like Open Horizon, making them accessible through natural language conversations. This blog post explores how to set up and use an Open Horizon MCP server, both locally and in IBM Cloud Code Engine, to enable AI-assisted edge computing management.

By the end of this guide, you'll understand: - What MCP is and why it's valuable for Open Horizon management - How to run the Open Horizon MCP server locally - How to deploy the server to IBM Cloud Code Engine and leverage its serverless capabilities - How to configure Claude Desktop to interact with your MCP server - How to use Claude to manage your Open Horizon environment through natural language

Let's dive in and explore how these technologies can work together to simplify edge computing management.

docs.title: Understanding MCP and Its Value Proposition
What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI models to interact with external tools and data sources in a structured way. Think of it as a "USB-C port for AI" - a standardized interface that allows AI assistants like Claude to connect to various systems and perform actions on your behalf.

Unlike traditional APIs that require developers to write code for each integration, MCP provides a consistent way for AI models to: - Discover available tools and capabilities - Execute operations with proper parameters - Receive structured responses - Maintain context across interactions

docs.title: Why MCP Matters for Open Horizon
docs.text:
Open Horizon is a powerful edge computing platform, but its management often requires specialized knowledge and command-line expertise. By exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server, we create several key benefits:

  1. Simplified Management: Users can interact with Open Horizon using natural language rather than memorizing complex commands.

  2. Knowledge Democratization: The expertise needed to manage edge devices becomes accessible to team members without specialized training.

  3. Operational Efficiency: Tasks that previously required multiple steps and careful syntax can be accomplished through simple conversational requests.

  4. Reduced Training Requirements: New team members can become productive faster, with the AI guiding them through complex operations.

  5. Better Decision Making: The AI can provide contextual explanations and recommendations based on the current state of your edge environment.

As stated in the Open Horizon MCP Server's value proposition document:

"Exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server enables AI agents to autonomously deploy, update, and manage containerized workloads across large numbers of distributed edge devices. Unlike traditional chatbots which rely on static knowledge and require explicit user requests, an MCP-enabled agent can manage and reason across thousands of edge devices simultaneously using real-time data to make dynamic decisions and trigger self-healing actions or re-task devices based on changing needs."

Now that we understand the value, let's see how to set up and use this powerful combination of technologies.

docs.title: Setting Up and Running the Open Horizon MCP Server Locally
docs.text: Running the Open Horizon MCP server locally is a great way to get started with AI-assisted edge computing management. It allows you to test the functionality in a controlled environment before deploying to production. Let's walk through the process step by step.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before we begin, make sure you have the following installed:

  • Node.js (v16 or higher)
  • npm (v7 or higher)
  • Git for cloning the repository
  • Access to an Open Horizon Exchange instance (you'll need the URL and credentials)

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
First, let's clone the Open Horizon MCP server repository:

git clone https://github.com/your-org/open-horizon-mcp-server.git
cd open-horizon-mcp-server

docs.title: Step 2: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Next, install the required Node.js dependencies:

npm install

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Environment Variables
docs.text:
The MCP server needs to connect to your Open Horizon Exchange instance. Create a .env file in the root directory with the following variables:

EXCHANGE_URL=<your-exchange-url>
EXCHANGE_ORG=<your-organization>
EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL=<your-base64-encoded-credentials>
PORT=3000

For example:

EXCHANGE_URL=http://open-horizon.example.com:3091/v1/orgs
EXCHANGE_ORG=myorg
EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL=bXlvcmcvbXl1c2VyOnBhc3N3b3Jk
PORT=3000

The EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL should be a Base64-encoded string of your username and password in the format org/user:password. You can generate this using:

echo -n "myorg/myuser:password" | base64

docs.title: Step 4: Build the Project
docs.text:
Compile the TypeScript code:

npm run build

docs.title: Step 5: Start the Server
docs.text:
Now you can start the MCP server:

npm start

You should see output similar to:

Open Horizon MCP Server listening on port: 3000

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Server is Running
docs.text:
To verify that the server is running correctly, you can check the health endpoint:

curl http://localhost:3000/health

You should receive a response like:

{"status":"healthy"}

docs.title: Understanding the Local Server Architecture
docs.text:
When running locally, the Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Listens on the configured port (default: 3000) for incoming MCP requests
  2. Maintains stateful sessions for each client connection
  3. Authenticates with the Open Horizon Exchange using the provided credentials
  4. Exposes tools for managing nodes, services, and policies

The server implements the Model Context Protocol, which allows AI assistants like Claude to discover and use the available tools. Each tool is registered with:

  • A unique name (e.g., list-nodes)
  • A description that helps the AI understand when to use it
  • A schema defining the expected parameters
  • A callback function that executes the actual API calls to the Open Horizon Exchange

This architecture makes it easy to extend the server with new capabilities by adding additional tools in the src/tools directory.

Now that we have our server running locally, let's look at how to deploy it to the cloud for production use.

docs.title: Deploying the Open Horizon MCP Server to IBM Cloud Code Engine
docs.text:
While running the MCP server locally is great for development and testing, deploying it to IBM Cloud Code Engine provides significant advantages for production use. Code Engine is a fully managed, serverless platform that's ideal for hosting MCP servers because it offers:

  • Zero infrastructure management - focus on your code, not servers
  • Automatic scaling - from zero to thousands of instances based on demand
  • Cost efficiency - pay only for what you use, with scale-to-zero when idle
  • Built-in security - secure container execution and network isolation
  • Global availability - deploy close to your users for lower latency

docs.title: Prerequisites for Cloud Deployment
docs.text:
Before deploying to IBM Cloud Code Engine, you'll need:

  • IBM Cloud account with Code Engine service enabled
  • IBM Cloud CLI installed and configured
  • Docker installed for building container images
  • Container Registry access (IBM Container Registry or another registry)

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare for Deployment
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server includes a deployment script in the bin/deploy.js file that simplifies the process. Before using it, you'll need to create a configuration file for your environment.

Create a file named .env-local.json in the root directory with your IBM Cloud Code Engine configuration:

{
  "dev": {
    "EXCHANGE_URL": "http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
    "EXCHANGE_ORG": "your-organization",
    "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
    "REGISTRY_ACCESS_SECRET": "your-registry-secret-name"
  },
  "prod": {
    "EXCHANGE_URL": "http://your-production-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
    "EXCHANGE_ORG": "your-organization",
    "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
    "REGISTRY_ACCESS_SECRET": "your-registry-secret-name"
  }
}

docs.title: Step 2: Build and Push the Docker Image
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server uses a multi-stage Dockerfile that creates an optimized container image. The deployment script handles building and pushing the image to your container registry.

To build for AMD64 architecture (most cloud environments):

npm run build:docker:amd64

For ARM64 architecture:

npm run build:docker:arm64

docs.title: Step 3: Deploy to IBM Cloud Code Engine
docs.text:
Once your Docker image is built and pushed to the registry, you can deploy to Code Engine using the provided script:

# Deploy to development environment
npm run deploy:dev

# Or deploy to production environment
npm run deploy:prod

These commands use the bin/deploy.js script, which:

  1. Builds the TypeScript code
  2. Creates a Docker image for the specified platform
  3. Tags the image with your registry information
  4. Pushes the image to the container registry
  5. Creates or updates the Code Engine application with the new image
  6. Sets environment variables from your .env-local.json file

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Deployment
docs.text:
After deployment, you can verify that your MCP server is running in Code Engine:

# Get the application URL
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appUrl

# Check the application status
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appInfo

# View application logs
npm run --appname=open-horizon-mcp-server-dev appLogs

The application URL will be something like:

https://open-horizon-mcp-server-dev.abcdefgh.us-south.codeengine.appdomain.cloud

You can verify the server is running by checking the health endpoint:

curl https://open-horizon-mcp-server-dev.abcdefgh.us-south.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/health

docs.title: Benefits of IBM Cloud Code Engine for MCP Servers
docs.text:
Deploying your Open Horizon MCP server to IBM Cloud Code Engine offers several key advantages:

  1. Elastic Scalability: Code Engine automatically scales your MCP server based on incoming requests. During periods of high demand (like when multiple users are interacting with Claude), it scales up to handle the load. When traffic decreases, it scales down to save costs—even to zero when not in use.

  2. Global Availability: Deploy your MCP server in multiple regions to reduce latency for users around the world. This is especially valuable for organizations with globally distributed edge devices and teams.

  3. Simplified Operations: Code Engine eliminates the need to manage servers, containers, or Kubernetes clusters. This reduces operational overhead and lets you focus on enhancing your MCP server's capabilities.

  4. Cost Optimization: With the pay-per-use model, you only pay for the actual compute resources consumed during request processing. For MCP servers that handle intermittent requests, this can result in significant cost savings compared to always-on deployments.

  5. Enterprise-Grade Security: Code Engine provides built-in security features like private networking, secrets management, and integration with IBM Cloud IAM for access control.

docs.title: Leveraging Code Engine Fleet (Coming Soon)
docs.text:
IBM Cloud Code Engine is introducing a new feature called "Fleet" that will be particularly valuable for MCP server deployments:

  1. Multi-Region Deployment: Fleet will allow you to deploy your MCP server across multiple regions with a single command, ensuring high availability and disaster recovery.

  2. Intelligent Traffic Routing: Requests will be automatically routed to the nearest healthy instance, reducing latency for users regardless of their location.

  3. Consistent Configuration: Fleet will maintain consistent configuration across all regions, simplifying management of your global MCP server deployment.

  4. Centralized Monitoring: Get a unified view of your MCP server's performance and usage across all regions, making it easier to identify and resolve issues.

When Code Engine Fleet becomes available, you'll be able to enhance your MCP server deployment with these capabilities, making it even more resilient and responsive for users around the world.

docs.title: Understanding the Cloud Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
When deployed to IBM Cloud Code Engine, the Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Runs as a containerized application using the Docker image we built
  2. Scales automatically based on incoming traffic (even to zero when not in use)
  3. Maintains high availability through Code Engine's infrastructure
  4. Securely stores credentials as environment variables
  5. Exposes a public HTTPS endpoint for AI assistants to connect to

The deployment uses several best practices:

  • Multi-stage Docker builds to minimize image size
  • Non-root user for improved security
  • Health checks for reliability monitoring
  • Environment-specific configurations for dev/test/prod separation

Now that our MCP server is deployed to the cloud, let's configure Claude Desktop to connect to it.

docs.title: Configuring Claude Desktop to Use the Open Horizon MCP Server
docs.text: Claude Desktop is a powerful AI assistant that can be extended with MCP servers to provide specialized capabilities. In this section, we'll configure Claude Desktop to connect to our Open Horizon MCP server, whether it's running locally or in the cloud.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before configuring Claude Desktop:

  • Install Claude Desktop on your computer (available for macOS and Windows)
  • Ensure your MCP server is running either locally or on IBM Cloud Code Engine
  • Have your Open Horizon Exchange credentials ready

docs.title: Step 1: Locate the Claude Desktop Configuration File
docs.text:
Claude Desktop stores its configuration in a JSON file. The location depends on your operating system:

  • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

docs.title: Step 2: Edit the Configuration File
docs.text:
Open the configuration file in your favorite text editor. You'll see a structure like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    // Existing MCP server configurations may be here
  }
}

docs.title: Step 3: Add the Open Horizon MCP Server Configuration
docs.text: Add a new entry for your Open Horizon MCP server. You have two options depending on where your server is running:

docs.title: Option A: For a Local MCP Server
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp-local": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "http://localhost:3000/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:your-organization",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:your-base64-encoded-credentials"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Option B: For a Cloud-Deployed MCP Server
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp-cloud": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "https://your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:your-organization",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:your-base64-encoded-credentials",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:Bearer your-auth-token"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Replace the placeholders with your actual values: - your-organization: Your Open Horizon organization name - your-exchange-url: The URL of your Open Horizon Exchange - your-base64-encoded-credentials: Your Base64-encoded credentials - your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud: The URL of your deployed Code Engine application - your-auth-token: If your MCP server requires authentication

docs.title: Step 4: Using Environment Variables for Sensitive Information
docs.text:
For better security, you can use environment variables for sensitive information:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "open-horizon-mcp": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", 
        "mcp-remote", 
        "https://your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/mcp",
        "--header",
        "exchange-org:playground",
        "--header",
        "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs",
        "--header",
        "exchange-credential:${EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL}",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:Bearer ${MCP_AUTH_TOKEN}"
      ],
      "env": {
        "EXCHANGE_CREDENTIAL": "your-base64-encoded-credentials",
        "MCP_AUTH_TOKEN": "your-auth-token"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Step 5: Save and Restart Claude Desktop
docs.text: After editing the configuration file, save it and restart Claude Desktop for the changes to take effect.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Connection
docs.text:
To verify that Claude Desktop is successfully connected to your Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Open Claude Desktop
  2. Start a new conversation
  3. Ask Claude to list the available nodes in your Open Horizon Exchange: "List all nodes registered in the Open Horizon Exchange"

If everything is configured correctly, Claude should use the MCP server to fetch and display the list of nodes.

docs.title: Understanding How Claude Desktop Connects to MCP Servers
docs.text:
When you configure an MCP server in Claude Desktop:

  1. Claude Desktop launches a local process using the specified command and args
  2. The mcp-remote tool establishes a connection to your MCP server
  3. Claude communicates with the MCP server through this connection
  4. The MCP server authenticates with the Open Horizon Exchange using the provided credentials
  5. Claude gains access to all the tools registered in the MCP server

This architecture allows Claude to securely interact with your Open Horizon environment without needing direct access to your credentials or systems.

Now that we've configured Claude Desktop to use our MCP server, let's explore how to use it to manage your Open Horizon environment.

docs.title: Using the Open Horizon MCP Server with Claude Desktop
docs.text: Now that we have our Open Horizon MCP server running and Claude Desktop configured to use it, let's explore how to leverage this powerful combination to manage your Open Horizon environment through natural language conversations.

docs.title: Available Tools and Capabilities
docs.text: The Open Horizon MCP server provides a rich set of tools that Claude can use to help you manage your edge computing environment. These tools are grouped into three main categories:

docs.title: Node Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-nodes: List all registered nodes
  • get-node-policy: Get the policy for a specific node
  • register-node-policy: Register a node with a policy
  • unregister-node: Remove a node from the Exchange

docs.title: Service Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-services: List all available services
  • get-service-details: Get detailed information about a service
  • publish-service: Publish a new service to the Exchange
  • delete-service: Remove a service from the Exchange
  • generate-service-definition: Create a service definition template

docs.title: Policy Management Tools
docs.text:
• list-deployment-policies: List all deployment policies
  • get-policy-details: Get detailed information about a policy
  • check-policy-deployments: See which workloads use a specific policy
  • check-policy-compatibility: Check which services are compatible with a policy
  • delete-policy: Remove a policy from the Exchange

docs.title: Example Conversations with Claude
docs.text: Let's look at some example conversations that demonstrate how to use Claude with the Open Horizon MCP server for common edge computing management tasks.

docs.title: Example 1: Exploring Your Edge Environment
docs.text:
You: I'm new to Open Horizon. Can you help me understand what's in my environment?

Claude: I'd be happy to help you explore your Open Horizon environment. Let's start by checking what nodes and services you have.

First, let me list all the nodes registered in your Open Horizon Exchange:

[Claude uses the list-nodes tool and displays the results]

These are all the edge devices registered in your environment. Now, let's see what services are available:

[Claude uses the list-services tool and displays the results]

Would you like me to explain any specific node or service in more detail?

docs.title: Example 2: Deploying a Service to Edge Nodes
docs.text:
You: I want to deploy the "hello-world" service to nodes with the "location:office" property.

Claude: I'll help you deploy the "hello-world" service to nodes with the "location:office" property. This involves creating a deployment policy that targets those specific nodes.

First, let me check if the "hello-world" service exists:

[Claude uses the get-service-details tool to verify the service exists]

Now, I'll create a deployment policy that targets nodes with the "location:office" property. Here's what the policy would look like:

{
  "label": "hello-world-office-deployment",
  "description": "Deploy hello-world to office locations",
  "service": {
    "name": "hello-world",
    "org": "your-organization",
    "arch": "amd64",
    "serviceVersions": [
      {
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "priority": {
          "priority_value": 1,
          "retries": 1,
          "retry_durations": 3600
        }
      }
    ]
  },
  "constraints": [
    "location == office"
  ]
}

Would you like me to publish this deployment policy to your Exchange?

[After your confirmation, Claude would use the appropriate tools to create and publish the policy]

docs.title: Example 3: Troubleshooting Node Registration
docs.text:
You: Node "edge-device-001" isn't running the services I expected. Can you help me troubleshoot?

Claude: I'll help you troubleshoot why "edge-device-001" isn't running the expected services. Let's investigate step by step.

First, let me check if the node is registered and get its policy:

[Claude uses the get-node-policy tool to retrieve the node's policy]

Now, let's see which services should be compatible with this node based on its policy:

[Claude uses the check-policy-compatibility tool to determine compatible services]

I notice that the node's policy has constraints that might be preventing the service from deploying. The node requires "memory >= 2048" but your service is configured for "memory >= 4096".

You have two options:
1. Update the node policy to accommodate the service requirements
2. Modify the service to work with the node's constraints

Would you like me to help you update the node policy?

docs.title: Best Practices for Working with Claude and the MCP Server
docs.text: To get the most out of Claude and the Open Horizon MCP server, follow these best practices:

docs.title: Beyond Claude: Using Other MCP Clients with the Open Horizon MCP Server
docs.text: While we've focused on using Claude Desktop with the Open Horizon MCP server in this guide, it's important to note that the Model Context Protocol is an open standard. This means that any MCP-compatible client can interact with your Open Horizon MCP server, not just Claude.

docs.title: Alternative MCP Clients
docs.text:
Here are some other MCP clients that you can use with your Open Horizon MCP server:

  1. Other Claude Interfaces: Beyond Claude Desktop, you can use other Claude interfaces that support MCP, such as Claude API with MCP extensions or Claude web interfaces that support MCP connections.

  2. Open Source MCP Clients: There are several open-source MCP client implementations that can connect to your server, including:

  3. MCP CLI tools for command-line interactions
  4. MCP client libraries for various programming languages (JavaScript, Python, etc.)

  5. Custom MCP clients built for specific use cases

  6. Other AI Assistants: As more AI assistants adopt the MCP standard, you'll be able to use them with your Open Horizon MCP server without any changes to the server itself.

docs.title: Integrating with Custom Applications
docs.text:
You can also build custom applications that use the MCP protocol to interact with your Open Horizon MCP server. This opens up possibilities for:

  1. Custom Web Interfaces: Build specialized web UIs for managing Open Horizon that use your MCP server as the backend.

  2. Mobile Applications: Create mobile apps that allow field technicians to manage edge devices through your MCP server.

  3. Integration with DevOps Tools: Connect your CI/CD pipelines to Open Horizon through the MCP server for automated deployments.

  4. Monitoring Dashboards: Build dashboards that use the MCP server to fetch and display real-time information about your edge devices.

docs.title: Example: Using the MCP CLI Tool
docs.text:
Here's a simple example of using an MCP CLI tool to interact with your Open Horizon MCP server:

# Install the MCP CLI tool
npm install -g mcp-cli

# Connect to your MCP server
mcp-cli connect https://your-app-name.region.codeengine.appdomain.cloud/mcp \
  --header "exchange-org:your-organization" \
  --header "exchange-url:http://your-exchange-url:3091/v1/orgs" \
  --header "exchange-credential:your-base64-encoded-credentials"

# List available tools
mcp-cli list-tools

# Execute a tool
mcp-cli execute list-nodes

docs.title: Benefits of the Open Protocol Approach
docs.text:
The fact that the Open Horizon MCP server uses an open protocol provides several benefits:

  1. Future-Proof: As new AI assistants and tools emerge that support MCP, they'll be able to work with your existing server.

  2. No Vendor Lock-In: You're not tied to any specific AI assistant or platform; you can switch between different MCP clients as needed.

  3. Extensibility: You can create custom clients tailored to specific user roles or use cases within your organization.

  4. Interoperability: Your MCP server can be part of a larger ecosystem of MCP-compatible tools and services.

By deploying your Open Horizon MCP server on IBM Cloud Code Engine, you're creating a flexible, scalable interface to your edge computing environment that can be accessed by a wide range of clients and integrated into various workflows and applications.

  1. Be Specific in Your Requests
  2. Instead of: "Show me the nodes"

  3. Use: "List all nodes registered in the Open Horizon Exchange"

  4. Include Key Terms

  5. Include terms like "nodes", "services", "policies", and "Open Horizon" in your requests

  6. Example: "Show me all the services in the Open Horizon Exchange"

  7. Provide Context

  8. When referring to specific nodes or services, provide their full names

  9. Example: "Get details about the service named 'hello-world' in the Open Horizon Exchange"

  10. Ask for Explanations

  11. Claude can explain Open Horizon concepts and the results it retrieves

  12. Example: "Explain what the constraints in this node policy mean"

  13. Build Complex Workflows Incrementally

  14. Start with simple requests and build up to more complex operations
  15. Let Claude guide you through multi-step processes

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
When using Claude with the Open Horizon MCP server, keep these security considerations in mind:

  1. Credential Management
  2. Store credentials securely using environment variables
  3. Regularly rotate your authentication tokens

  4. Use the minimum required permissions for your Exchange credentials

  5. Access Control

  6. Be mindful of who has access to your Claude Desktop with the MCP configuration

  7. Consider using separate credentials with limited permissions for demonstration purposes

  8. Sensitive Operations

  9. Double-check Claude's suggestions before confirming destructive operations
  10. Consider implementing additional approval workflows for critical changes

By following these practices, you can safely and effectively use Claude with the Open Horizon MCP server to manage your edge computing environment.

docs.title: Recap: The Power of Combining Open Horizon, MCP, Claude, and IBM CodeEngine
docs.text:
In this blog post, we've explored how to combine four powerful technologies:

  1. Open Horizon: A robust edge computing platform for managing distributed devices
  2. Model Context Protocol (MCP): A standardized interface for AI-tool interactions
  3. Claude: An advanced AI assistant capable of natural language understanding
  4. IBM Cloud Code Engine: A serverless platform that provides scalable, cost-effective hosting

Together, these technologies transform how we manage edge computing environments. By exposing Open Horizon's capabilities through an MCP server deployed on IBM Cloud Code Engine and connecting Claude to it, we've created a system that allows anyone to manage complex edge computing operations through simple, natural language conversations.

The benefits of this approach include:

  • Simplified management through conversational interfaces
  • Democratized access to powerful edge computing capabilities
  • Reduced training requirements for new team members
  • Improved operational efficiency through AI assistance
  • Better decision making with contextual insights
  • Cost-effective scaling with Code Engine's serverless architecture
  • Global availability for distributed teams and edge devices

docs.title: Beyond the Basics: Extending the Open Horizon MCP Server
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server we've explored is just the beginning. Here are some ways you could extend it:

  1. Add Custom Tools: Create new tools for specific use cases in your organization typescript // Example: Create a tool to analyze node health export function registerNodeHealthTool(server: McpServer) { server.tool( 'analyze-node-health', 'Analyze the health of a specific node', { nodeId: z.string().describe('ID of the node to analyze') }, async (params, context) => { // Implementation here } ); }

  2. Integrate with Monitoring Systems: Connect the MCP server to your monitoring infrastructure to provide real-time insights typescript // Example: Create a resource that fetches monitoring data server.resource('node-metrics', 'Node performance metrics', async () => { // Fetch metrics from your monitoring system return { contents: [ { text: metricsData, uri: 'node-metrics', mimeType: 'text/plain' } ] }; });

  3. Implement Automated Workflows: Create tools that perform complex sequences of operations typescript // Example: Create a tool to deploy a service to all nodes in a region export function registerRegionalDeploymentTool(server: McpServer) { server.tool( 'deploy-to-region', 'Deploy a service to all nodes in a specific region', { serviceName: z.string().describe('Name of the service to deploy'), region: z.string().describe('Region to deploy to') }, async (params, context) => { // Implementation here } ); }

docs.title: Future Directions with IBM Cloud Code Engine
docs.text:
As IBM Cloud Code Engine continues to evolve, we can expect even more powerful capabilities for hosting MCP servers:

  1. Global Fleet Deployments: Deploy your MCP server across multiple regions with Code Engine Fleet for improved availability and reduced latency

  2. Integrated Observability: Leverage IBM Cloud Monitoring and Logging services for comprehensive visibility into your MCP server's performance

  3. Event-Driven Architecture: Connect your MCP server to event sources like IBM Event Streams for real-time responses to changes in your environment

  4. Hybrid Cloud Integration: Extend your MCP server to interact with systems across public cloud, private cloud, and on-premises environments

docs.title: Future Directions for AI-Assisted Edge Computing
docs.text:
As MCP and AI assistants continue to evolve, we can expect even more powerful capabilities for managing edge computing environments:

  1. Autonomous Management: AI agents that can proactively monitor and manage edge devices with minimal human intervention

  2. Multi-Agent Collaboration: Multiple specialized AI agents working together to manage different aspects of your edge computing environment

  3. Predictive Maintenance: AI systems that can predict issues before they occur and take preventive actions

  4. Natural Language Policy Definition: Creating and managing policies through conversational interfaces rather than JSON files

  5. Cross-Platform Integration: Extending the MCP approach to integrate with other systems beyond Open Horizon

docs.title: Getting Involved
docs.text:
The Open Horizon MCP server is an open-source project, and contributions are welcome. Here are some ways to get involved:

  1. Try it out: Set up the server and experiment with using Claude to manage your Open Horizon environment

  2. Contribute: Add new tools, fix bugs, or improve documentation

  3. Share your experience: Write about your use cases and how this approach has helped your organization

  4. Join the community: Connect with other users and developers working on similar projects

docs.title: Final Thoughts
docs.text:
The combination of Open Horizon, MCP, Claude, and IBM Cloud Code Engine represents a significant step forward in making edge computing more accessible and manageable. By enabling natural language interactions with complex systems through a scalable, serverless architecture, we're removing barriers to adoption and empowering more people to leverage the power of edge computing.

As you implement this solution in your own environment, remember that the goal is not just to make existing operations easier, but to enable new possibilities that weren't practical before. With AI-assisted management and serverless deployment, you can scale your edge computing initiatives further and faster than ever before.

Happy edge computing!

docs.title: service-postgresql
docs.text: This is an Open Horizon configuration to deploy a vanilla instance of the open-source PostgreSQL database software. This service is intended to be used as an edge service that provides PostgreSQL database functionality to other services running on the same edge node. It is not intended to be a production-ready database server, but rather a lightweight way to provide a database for development or testing purposes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Management Hub: Install the Open Horizon Management Hub or have access to an existing hub in order to publish this service and register your edge node. You may also choose to use a downstream commercial distribution based on Open Horizon, such as IBM's Edge Application Manager. If you'd like to use the Open Horizon community hub, you may apply for a temporary account and have credentials sent to you.

Edge Node: You will need an x86 computer running Linux or macOS, or a Raspberry Pi computer (arm64) running Raspberry Pi OS or Ubuntu to install and use the Postgres database service as deployed by Open Horizon. You will need to install the Open Horizon agent software, anax, on the edge node and register it with a hub.

Optional utilities to install: With brew on macOS (you may need to install that as well), apt-get on Ubuntu or Raspberry Pi OS, yum on Fedora, install gcc, make, git, jq, curl, net-tools. Not all of those may exist on all platforms, and some may already be installed. But reflexively installing those has proven helpful in having the right tools available when you need them.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Clone the service-postgresql GitHub repo from a terminal prompt on the edge node and enter the folder where the artifacts were copied.

NOTE: This assumes that git has been installed on the edge node.

shell git clone https://github.com/open-horizon-services/service-postgresql.git cd service-postgresql

Run make clean to confirm that the "make" utility is installed and working.

Confirm that you have the Open Horizon agent installed by using the CLI to check the version:

shell hzn version

It should return values for both the CLI and the Agent (actual version numbers may vary from those shown):

text Horizon CLI version: 2.30.0-744 Horizon Agent version: 2.30.0-744

If it returns "Command not found", then the Open Horizon agent is not installed.

If it returns a version for the CLI but not the agent, then the agent is installed but not running. You may run it with systemctl horizon start on Linux or horizon-container start on macOS.

Check that the agent is in an unconfigured state, and that it can communicate with a hub. If you have the jq utility installed, run hzn node list | jq '.configstate.state' and check that the value returned is "unconfigured". If not, running make agent-stop or hzn unregister -f will put the agent in an unconfigured state. Run hzn node list | jq '.configuration' and check that the JSON returned shows values for the "exchange_version" property, as well as the "exchange_api" and "mms_api" properties showing URLs. If those do not, then the agent is not configured to communicate with a hub. If you do not have jq installed, run hzn node list and eyeball the sections mentioned above.

NOTE: If "exchange_version" is showing an empty value, you will not be able to publish and run the service. The only fix found to this condition thus far is to re-install the agent using these instructions:

hzn unregister -f # to ensure that the node is unregistered
systemctl horizon stop # for Linux, or "horizon-container stop" on macOS
export HZN_ORG_ID=myorg   # or whatever you customized it to
export HZN_EXCHANGE_USER_AUTH=admin:<admin-pw>   # use the pw deploy-mgmt-hub.sh displayed
export HZN_FSS_CSSURL=http://<mgmt-hub-ip>:9443/
curl -sSL https://github.com/open-horizon/anax/releases/latest/download/agent-install.sh | bash -s -- -i anax: -k css: -c css: -p IBM/pattern-ibm.helloworld -w '*' -T 120

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To manually run PostgreSQL locally as a test, enter make. Running make attach will connect you to a prompt running inside the container, and you can end that session by entering exit. When you are done, run make stop in the terminal to end the test.

Populate the Secrets Manager before publishing services:

hzn sm secret add --secretKey=user --secretDetail=<username> secret_user
hzn sm secret add --secretKey=password --secretDetail=<password> secret_password
hzn sm secret add --secretKey=db --secretDetail=<databaseName> secret_db

The first time you intend to run this on a host, run sudo -sE make init. This will create the volume that persists data across container restarts. It will also create the directory that the database is stored in and ensure it has the proper permissions.

If you are not running as root, you must add the current user account to the docker group so that it can run docker commands without sudo: sudo usermod -a -G docker $USER.

To create the service definition, publish it to the hub, and then form an agreement to download and run PostgreSQL, enter make publish. When installation is complete and an agreement has been formed, exit the watch command with Control-C.

docs.title: Advanced details
docs.text: NOTE: If you are planning to run this on the same host as the exchange, there will be a port conflict. Change the port numbers (5432) in both the Makefile and the service.definition.json before publishing and using.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
The Makefile includes several targets to assist you in inspecting what is happening to see if they match your expectations. They include:

make log to see both the event logs and the service logs.

make check to see the values in your environment variables and how they compare to the default values. It will also show the service definition file with those values filled in.

make deploy-check to see if the properties and constraints that you've configured match each other to potentially form an agreement.

make test to see if the web server is responding.

make attach to connect to the running container and open a shell inside it.

Note The service-postgresql container by default runs in un-privileged mode.

docs.title: All Makefile targets
docs.text:
• default - init run browse
  • init - optionally create the docker volume
  • run - manually run the postgres container locally as a test
  • check - view current settings
  • stop - halt a locally-run container
  • dev - manually run postgresql locally and connect to a terminal in the container
  • attach - connect to a terminal in the postgresql container
  • test - request the web UI from the terminal to confirm that it is running and available
  • clean - remove the container image and docker volume
  • distclean - clean (see above) AND unregister the node and remove the service files from the hub
  • build - N/A
  • push - N/A
  • publish-service - Publish the service definition file to the hub in your organization
  • remove-service - Remove the service definition file from the hub in your organization
  • publish-deployment-policy - Publish a deployment policy for the service to the hub in your org
  • remove-deployment-policy - Remove a deployment policy for the service from the hub in your org
  • agent-run - register your agent's node policy with the hub
  • publish - Publish the service def, deployment policy, and then register your agent
  • agent-stop - unregister your agent with the hub, halting all agreements and stopping containers
  • deploy-check - confirm that a registered agent is compatible with the service and deployment
  • log - check the agent event logs

docs.title: sms-me
docs.text:
Sends an SMS message to the specified phone (SMS) number stating the IP address of the specified interface.

Uses the Sinch service. Visit that site and create a free account, then get your SERVICE_PLAN_ID, API_TOKEN, and a SENDER_SMS_NUMBER, that you will need below.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
1. Edit the Makefie to add:
SERVICE_PLAN_ID (your sinch plan ID)
API_TOKEN (your sinch API token)
SENDER_SMS_NUMBER (any of the virtual numbers or real numbers on your sinch account)
INTERFACE_NAME (the network interface whose IP address you want to know)
TARGET_SMS_NUMBER (the target SMS number where the message will be sent)

  1. Then run make build, and

  2. Then run make run

docs.title: Notes:
docs.text:
This container will send the LAN IP address message once on startup, then it will sleep forever. If it is restarted (e.g., after a power cycle) it will send a new message (possibly with a new IP address since the local DHCP server may assign it a new one). This code is dumber than you might want it to be since it does not monitor the IP address to see if it has changed over time. But a reboot should fix it if its IP address changes. If anyone wanted to submit a PR that does that monitoring and automates sending a new message, that would be cool. :-)

The docker run command must include the --net=host flag so the container can discern the LAN IP address assigned to the specified INTERFACE_NAME.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
service-speak-ip is a lightweight Open Horizon microservice designed to audibly announce the LAN IP address of its host device (such as a Raspberry Pi) every 30 seconds. It uses the espeak tool to convert the IP address to speech, making it easy to identify the device's network address without needing a display or SSH access. This service is ideal for IoT and edge computing scenarios where quick, hands-free identification of a device's IP is useful.

It does this over and over forever, every 30 seconds.

Of course, if you wish to hear the speech, you will need to plug in some earphones/headphones or if you have configured your Raspberry Pi to use only the HDMI for audio output, then you will need to connect an HDMI cable to something that can emit audio.

This little example uses the default English espeak voice for this (which is pretty horrible), and sends it a text string that looks similar to this:

Your eye pee address is 1 9 2 dot 1 6 8 dot 1 dot 1 2 3

The espeak tool can pronounce many other languages, so hack away if you want that. Here is some documentation: http://espeak.sourceforge.net/docindex.html

By default it only looks at the eth0 interface. If yu plan to use WiFi then edit the Makefile to specify wlan0 as the INTERFACE_NAME. If deploying wiith Open Horizon, set the INTERFACE_NAME as a Service variable.

Of course, specifying the INTERFACE_NAME is inconvenient. You could do something better, like determine the hosts's "default route" and then find the host interface that was on that network, and then announce the IP address of that interface. If you did that, then then you would not need to pass any INTERFACE_NAME at all. But I was tooo lazy to code that! :-)

This has currently only been tested on a few Raspberry Pi models.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Hardware: Raspberry Pi (or compatible Linux device) with audio output (headphones, speakers, or HDMI audio)
  • Software:
  • Docker (for containerized deployment)
  • Python 3
  • espeak (speech synthesis)
  • netifaces Python package
  • Environment Variables:
  • INTERFACE_NAME (default: eth0) — The network interface whose IP address will be spoken. Set to wlan0 for WiFi, or another interface as needed.

docs.title: Docker (Recommended)
docs.text:
1. Clone this repository: sh git clone https://github.com/open-horizon-services/service-speak-ip.git cd service-speak-ip
  2. Build the Docker image: sh docker build -t speak-ip:latest .

docs.title: Local (Direct Python)
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies: sh sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip espeak pip3 install netifaces
  2. (Optional) Set the INTERFACE_NAME environment variable: sh export INTERFACE_NAME=eth0 # or wlan0, etc.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Run the service in a container (replace eth0 with your interface if needed):

docker run -d \
  --name speak-ip \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --device /dev/snd \
  --net=host \
  -e INTERFACE_NAME=eth0 \
  speak-ip:latest

docs.title: Local (Direct Python)
docs.text:
Run the service directly (ensure dependencies are installed):

python3 speak-ip.py

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Attach a speaker or headphones to your device.
  • The service will announce the IP address every 30 seconds.
  • To change the interface, set the INTERFACE_NAME environment variable before running.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: • INTERFACE_NAME: The network interface to monitor (default: eth0). Set to wlan0 for WiFi or another interface as needed.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
• The service uses the default English espeak voice. You can modify speak-ip.py to use a different language or voice supported by espeak.
  • By default, the service only looks at the specified interface. For more advanced detection (e.g., auto-detecting the default route), you can enhance the script as described in the comments.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• The service retrieves the IPv4 address of the specified interface using the netifaces Python package.
  • It converts the IP address into a "speakable" string (e.g., 1 9 2 dot 1 6 8 dot 1 dot 1 2 3).
  • The espeak tool is used to audibly announce the IP address every 30 seconds.

docs.title: skills-open-horizon
docs.text: AI-assisted skills for bootstrapping and managing Open Horizon service repositories. Drop these into any project to let your ML-assisted IDE scaffold license files, .gitignore, MAINTAINERS.md, Makefile, and README.md using conversational commands.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Install
  • Prerequisites
  • Repository management Skills
  • Initialize a Repository
  • Contributing
  • Open Horizon admin Skills
  • License

docs.title: Install skills into your project
docs.text:
Run this one-liner from the root of your target repository to download and execute the installer script. It clones this repository into a temporary directory, copies the .agent folder into your project, then removes the temporary directory.

bash <(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-horizon-services/skills-open-horizon/main/install-skills.sh)

Tip: The script creates .agent/ in your current working directory, so run it from your repository root.

docs.title: Install Open Spec
docs.text:
Requires NodeJS 20.19.0+ to install globally, which is recommended.

# To install globally
npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest

# To verify
openspec --version

Note: It can also be run from a Docker container instead of installed.

docs.title: (Fork and) clone your repository
docs.text:
cd your-repository-folder
openspec init
# choose your editor and [Enter]

docs.title: Optionally install Obsidian
docs.text:
Install the Obsidian desktop app and activate the CLI, then run the init-obsidian skill to set up an Obsidian vault for managing memories and keeping your context clean.

For full instructions refer to .agent/skills/init-obsidian/SKILL.md.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Skill Description init-license Create or replace a LICENSE.md (Apache 2.0, MIT, MPL, ISC) with copyright placeholders populated from git config init-gitignore Scan the codebase, detect languages and frameworks, and compose a .gitignore with user approval init-readme Create a README.md with standard Open Horizon sections or audit an existing one for missing sections init-maintainers Create or update MAINTAINERS.md in the canonical Open Horizon table format init-makefile Stub a Makefile with standard Open Horizon targets for services using third-party containers init-obsidian Set up Obsidian CLI and install skills for memory management gitignore-snippets Reference library of .gitignore snippets for common stacks (Node, Python, Java, Go, etc.)

docs.title: Initialize the repository
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init repo. It will then go through all the skills listed above. If that doesn't work, reference the @init-repo.md workflow file and instruct the tool to read the contents and follow the guidance. If you do not want to run all of the skills at one go, manually run each skill that you do want to execute.

docs.title: LICENSE.md
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init license. It will create a license file if one does not exist, populate the contents with a preferred license of your choice if the file is empty, and it will fill in license placeholders if they are not populated.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init gitignore. It will scan the codebase and propose to populate the .gitignore file with sane defaults per best practices.

docs.title: README.md
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init readme to create a new README.md with standard Open Horizon sections (shields, prerequisites, installation, usage, debugging, Makefile targets), or to audit an existing one and recommend missing sections.

docs.title: MAINTAINERS.md
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init maintainers. It will extract your name, github ID, and email address from git defaults and populate the structure. It will give you the option of adding more maintainers, and adding an emeritus section.

docs.title: Makefile stub
docs.text: Ask your ML-assisted IDE to init makefile. It will stub out the makefile based on the current repository information and create default targets. Test each target to confirm correct functionality.

docs.title: Optionals
docs.text:
When you're ready to begin working on the code, start in a terminal at the root directory of your repository and initialize the project plan with the editor of your choice. For example, if you're using bob, then type:

openspec init --tools bob

Then start your editor:

bob

And then describe the work you'd like to begin as an Open Spec proposal using the /opsx-propose slash command. This could be text straight from an issue, or a short feature description. If needed, paste the URL of the github issue or description. For example:

/opsx-propose “Work on adding the optional section to the documentation described in the GitHub issue https://github.com/open-horizon-services/skills-open-horizon/issues/5”

Review what was created. When you're satisfied with the results, begin development with the Open Spec apply slash command:

/opsx-apply

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. Open an issue at github.com/open-horizon-services/skills-open-horizon.

New skills should follow the existing conventions: a directory under .agent/skills/{skill-name}/ containing a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description), step-by-step instructions, guardrails, and example output. Workflows live in .agent/workflows/*.md.

docs.title: oh-* SKILL.md files
docs.text:
Open Horizon-specific administration and management skills should use the oh- prefix in their skill directory name (for example: .agent/skills/oh-init-service/SKILL.md). This naming convention makes it easy to discover and filter Open Horizon skills in tooling and menus.

Location

  • Place Open Horizon skills at: .agent/skills/oh-<skill-name>/SKILL.md

Required frontmatter

Include YAML frontmatter at the top of the SKILL.md with at least the following fields:

  • name: human-readable skill identifier (string)
  • description: short summary of what the skill does (string)
  • tags: (optional) array of tags; include oh or open-horizon to aid discovery

Example frontmatter

---
name: oh-init-service
description: "Initialize an Open Horizon service repository with standard files and metadata"
tags:
  - oh
  - open-horizon
---

Content guidelines

  • Provide clear, step-by-step instructions the ML-assisted IDE or human operators can follow.
  • Include example commands and expected outputs so users can validate the skill's behavior.
  • Add guardrails that state what the skill will not modify or any assumptions it makes.
  • Reference related workflow files in .agent/workflows/ when appropriate.
  • Keep examples idempotent and safe to run in local development environments.

Discovery and usage

  • Installer and discovery tooling look for the oh- prefix to present Open Horizon skills separately from general skills. Follow the naming convention to ensure your skill appears in Open Horizon-specific filters and menus.
  • Avoid committing secrets or environment-specific configuration in SKILL.md files; keep them generic and instructional.

If adding a new Open Horizon skill, follow these conventions and consider opening a short PR that documents the skill's purpose and usage so others can discover and reuse it.
